standard.title: Post-War Global Influences on Australian Society
standard.description: the effects of significant post–Second World War world events, ideas and developments on Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined post-war reconstruction and Australia's strategic reorientation in AC9HH10K05, including the 'populate or perish' migration drive and the Colombo Plan. They understand push and pull factors in migration from general geographic study. They have not yet examined the specific waves of post-war migration in detail, the policy mechanisms governing migration, or the push factors driving each wave.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the effects of significant post-war world events and developments on Australian society, including the causes and nature of successive waves of migration and the government policies that shaped them.

nodes.label: Push and pull factors as an analytical framework
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply a push-pull framework to explain why migration occurs, distinguishing factors that drive people from their home countries from factors that attract them to Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain the push-pull framework and apply it to at least one post-war migration wave with at least two push and two pull factors.
nodes.typical_width: Students establish push factors (war, economic collapse, political persecution, social upheaval) and pull factors (Australia's peaceful democracy, economic opportunity, established migrant communities, government recruitment); apply the framework to the post-war European migration context; explain why push-pull analysis is more analytically powerful than simply listing migration events.
wider: Examine how push and pull factors interact — analysing cases where the same global event (e.g. the Holocaust, the Vietnam War) operates as a push factor for some migrants and shapes Australia's pull factors through policy responses
Investigate how the relative weight of push versus pull factors varies across migration waves — and what this reveals about the different kinds of migration (refugee, economic, family reunion)
nodes.hinge_reason: The push-pull framework is the analytical tool N2–N4 apply to successive migration waves. Students who lack it approach migration as a list of events rather than a pattern of causes. Without the framework, they cannot explain why each wave occurred when it did or compare waves analytically.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe migration as simply 'people moving to Australia' without causal analysis. Making the push-pull distinction explicit — and practising its application to a clear case before applying it to successive waves — is the scaffold for N2–N4.

success_criteria: Explains the push-pull framework and distinguishes the two types of factor
Applies it to at least one post-war migration context with at least two push and two pull factors
Explains why push-pull analysis is more useful than listing migration events

nodes.label: Post-war European migration — causes and government policy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the causes of post-war European migration to Australia and describe the government policies that shaped it, including the 'populate or perish' and 'White Australia' policies.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two push factors driving post-war European migration and describe the 'populate or perish' policy and its rationale.
nodes.typical_width: Students apply the push-pull framework to post-war European migration (1940s–1960s) — push factors including the Holocaust, war devastation, displacement camps, economic collapse; pull factors including Australian recruitment, assisted passage, and the 'populate or perish' strategic imperative; explain the 'White Australia' policy as the racial boundary within which migration was shaped; describe the Displaced Persons programme and bilateral agreements with European countries; explain the social impact of mass European migration on Australian society.
wider: Examine the experience of specific migrant groups — Italian, Greek, Polish, Baltic — and how their reception in Australia reflected both welcome and discrimination, analysing the gap between recruitment policy and social reality

Investigate the Child Migration scheme (1922–1967) as a distinct and contested form of migration — examining the experiences of child migrants and the long-term consequences that led to the 2009 apology

response_modes.reason: Students need a solid factual account of the first migration wave — its causes, scale, and policy context — before the pattern of changing waves in N3 is analytically accessible.

success_criteria: Explains at least two push factors driving post-war European migration with specific evidence
Describes the 'populate or perish' policy and explains its strategic rationale
Explains the role of the 'White Australia' policy as a boundary condition on post-war migration

nodes.label: Successive migration waves — changing sources and causes
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the nature of successive post-war migration waves and explain the changing push factors and policy shifts that produced each wave.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two distinct migration waves after the initial European wave and explain the push factors driving each.
nodes.typical_width: Students trace the successive waves — Asian migration from the 1970s onwards (Vietnam War refugees, then broader Asian economic migration), Middle Eastern migration from the 1980s–1990s, Indian migration from the 1990s–2000s, African migration from the 2000s; explain the push factors driving each wave (Vietnam War communist victory, Lebanese civil war, economic opportunity, conflict and persecution); explain the policy shifts that enabled each wave — dismantling of the White Australia policy across the late 1960s to 1973.
wider: Examine the Vietnamese refugee wave as a case study in the relationship between foreign policy and migration — analysing how Australia's involvement in the Vietnam War created a moral and political obligation to accept Vietnamese refugees

Compare the reception of successive waves — examining how public attitudes to migration shifted as the source countries changed from European to Asian to Middle Eastern, and what drove those attitudinal shifts
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Vietnamese refugee case study and the comparison of reception across waves offer rich analytical opportunities connecting K07 to K08's changing perspectives content. The foreign policy–migration relationship is a genuinely transferable analytical frame.

response_modes.reason: Examining multiple waves with their distinct push factors prevents students from treating post-war migration as a single uniform phenomenon. Each wave has its own causal logic and policy context; building the full repertoire is necessary before K08's attitudes-and-change analysis.

success_criteria: Describes at least two distinct migration waves after the initial European wave with specific evidence
Explains the push factors driving each identified wave
Explains at least one policy shift that enabled a new wave of migration

nodes.label: Effects of migration on Australian society
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the effects of successive migration waves on Australian society — economic, social, cultural, and demographic — evaluating the overall significance of migration to Australia's post-war development.
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain at least two effects of post-war migration on Australian society across different domains (economic, social, or cultural).
nodes.typical_width: Students analyse the demographic transformation of Australia through successive waves; examine economic effects (workforce expansion, skills contribution, entrepreneurship); examine social and cultural effects (cuisine, religion, language, community institutions, arts); evaluate the significance of migration to Australia's post-war development as a whole; connect to K08's content on how migration transformed Australian identity and prompted the debate over multiculturalism.
wider: Examine the contribution of specific migrant communities to Australian cultural and economic life — using case studies to move beyond generalisation
Evaluate whether 'multiculturalism' accurately describes Australia's post-war migration experience, or whether it obscures the ongoing tensions and inequalities that migration produced
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The evaluation of multiculturalism as a concept versus a lived reality is a rich analytical question that connects K07 forward to K08 and K13 and invites genuine argument rather than description.

response_modes.reason: This node draws together the push-pull framework (N1), the policy context (N2), and the wave chronology (N3) into an evaluative account of migration's overall significance. Synthesis tasks requiring students to argue across multiple domains work well here.

success_criteria: Explains at least two effects of post-war migration on Australian society across different domains
Evaluates the overall significance of migration to Australia's post-war development
Connects migration's effects to the emergence of multiculturalism as a social and political concept
